title: What If Petrov Had Reported the Launch?
topic: What if Petrov had reported the launch? (1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm)
mechanism: A satellite early-warning system mistook sunlight glinting off high clouds for five missile launches; the duty officer reasoned that a real first strike would be hundreds of missiles and ground radar showed nothing, so he reported a system fault instead of passing the warning up a chain that would have had only minutes to decide.

beats.hook: In 1983 a computer told one Soviet officer that American missiles were coming; he decided it was wrong. Camera glides through the bunker onto the glowing LAUNCH board with Petrov at the console.
beats.but: Weeks after the Korean airliner was shot down, Moscow fears an American first strike.
beats.then: The siren: one missile, another, five; the officer asks what to report; Petrov's job is to pass it up the chain.
beats.conflict: Moscow would have minutes to decide.
beats.pivot: You see, a real first strike would be hundreds of missiles, not five, and ground radar had nothing: he reports a system fault and waits.
beats.so: So what if he had reported it: the warning climbs to the Kremlin; some say other checks would have stopped it; nobody wants to find out. His reward was a reprimand and fifteen years of secrecy.
beats.closing: Petrov later called it fifty-fifty. He bet the computer was wrong. And he was right.
